2.4	
Fair value measurement
	
Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between 
market participants at the measurement date, regardless of whether that price is directly observable or estimated using another 
valuation technique. In estimating the fair value of an asset or a liability, the Group takes into account the characteristics of the 
asset or liability if market participants would take those characteristics into account when pricing the asset or liability at the 
measurement date. Fair value for measurement and/or disclosure purposes in these financial statements is determined on such 
a basis, except for share-based payment transactions that are within the scope of Ind AS 102, leasing transactions that are 
within the scope of Ind AS 116, and measurements that have some similarities to fair value but are not fair value, such as net 
realisable value in Ind AS 2 or value in use in Ind AS 36.
	
In addition, for financial reporting purposes, fair value measurements are categorized into Level 1, 2, or 3 based on the degree to 
which the inputs to the fair value measurements are observable and the significance of the inputs to the fair value measurement

Level 1 inputs are quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets for identical assets or liabilities that the entity can access 
at the measurement date;

Level 2 inputs are inputs other than quoted prices included within Level 1, that are observable for the asset or liability, 
either directly or indirectly; and
•	
Level 3 inputs are unobservable inputs for the asset or liability.

2.10	
Leases
	
As a Lessee: The Group, at the inception of a contract, assesses whether the contract is a lease or not lease. A contract is, 
or contains, a lease if the contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a time in exchange for a 
consideration.
	
The Group recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability at the lease commencement date. The right-of-use asset is 
initially measured at cost, which comprises the initial amount of the lease liability adjusted for any lease payments made at 
or before the commencement date, plus any initial direct costs incurred and an estimate of costs to dismantle and remove the 
underlying asset or to restore the underlying asset or the site on which it is located, less any lease incentives received.
	
The right-of-use asset is subsequently depreciated using the straight-line basis over the shorter of the lease term and the 
estimated useful life of the assets from the commencement date to the end of the lease term. In addition, the right-of-use asset 
is periodically reduced by impairment losses, if any, and adjusted for certain re-measurements of the lease liability.
	
The Average lease term for major categories of leasehold assets are as follows: -

At the commencement date of the lease, the Group recognises lease liabilities measured at the present value of lease payments 
to be made over the lease term. The lease payments include fixed payments (including in substance fixed payments) less any 
lease incentives receivable, variable lease payments that depend on an index or a rate, and amounts expected to be paid under 
residual value guarantees. The lease payments also include the exercise price of a purchase option reasonably certain to be 
exercised by the Group and payments of penalties for terminating the lease, if the lease term reflects the Group exercising the 
option to terminate. Variable lease payments that do not depend on an index or a rate are recognised as expenses (unless they 
are incurred to produce inventories) in the period in which the event or condition that triggers the payment occurs.
	
In calculating the present value of lease payments, the Group uses its incremental borrowing rate at the lease commencement 
date because the interest rate implicit in the lease is not readily determinable. After the commencement date, the amount 
of lease liabilities is increased to reflect the accretion of interest and reduced for the lease payments made. In addition, the 
carrying amount of lease liabilities is remeasured if there is a modification, a change in the lease term, a change in the lease 
payments (e.g., changes to future payments resulting from a change in an index or rate used to determine such lease payments) 
or a change in the assessment of an option to purchase the underlying asset.
	
The Group has elected not to recognise right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for short-term leases that have a lease term of 
12 months or less and leases of low-value assets. The Group recognises the lease payments associated with these leases as 
an expense over the lease term.
2.11	
Functional and presentation currency
	
Items included in the financial statements of the Group are measured using the currency of the primary economic environment 
in which these entities operate (i.e., the “functional currency”). The financial statements are presented in Indian Rupee (₹), the 
national currency of India, which is the functional currency of the Group and rounded to the nearest lakhs.
2.12	
Foreign currencies
	
Foreign currency transactions are recorded at exchange rates prevailing on the date of the transaction or at rates that closely 
approximate the rate at the date of transactions. The date of transaction for the purpose of determining the exchange rate 
on initial recognition of the related asset, expense or income (part of it) is the date on which the entity initially recognises 
the non-monetary asset or non-monetary liability arising from payment or receipt of advance consideration. Foreign currency 
denominated monetary assets and liabilities are restated into the functional currency using exchange rates prevailing on the 
balance sheet date. Gains and losses arising on settlement and restatement of foreign currency denominated monetary assets 
and liabilities are recognised in the statement of profit and loss. Non-monetary assets and liabilities that are measured in terms 
of historical cost in foreign currencies are not translated.
	
For the purposes of presenting the consolidated financial statements assets and liabilities of Group’s foreign operations with 
functional currency different from the Group are translated into Group’s functional currency i.e. INR using exchange rates 
prevailing at the end of each reporting period. Income and expense items are translated at the average exchange rates for the 
period, unless exchange rates fluctuate significantly during that period, in which case the exchange rates at the dates of the 
transactions are used.
	
Exchange differences arising, if any are recognised in other comprehensive income and accumulated in equity.
	
On the disposal of foreign operation, all of the exchange differences accumulated in equity in respect of that operation 
attributable to the owners of the company are reclassified to the statement of profit and loss.

Revenue recognition
	
Revenue from contracts with customers is recognised when control of the goods or services are transferred to the customer at 
an amount that reflects the consideration to which the Group expects to be entitled in exchange for those goods or services. 
The Group has generally concluded that it is the principal in its revenue arrangements, because it typically controls the goods

Sale of goods is recognised net of returns, trade discounts, volume discounts, scheme allowances and price concessions

for discounts/incentives are estimated using the most likely method based on accumulated experience and underlying 
schemes and agreements with customers (Refer para 2.30.1). The performance obligation in the case of sale of goods

Further, as required by Ind AS 20, the Group matches subsidy income with related costs which the subsidy is intended to

c)	
Income from services rendered is recognised based on the agreements/arrangements with the concerned parties and

d)

e)

f)

performs by transferring goods or services to a customer before the Customer pays consideration or before payment 
is due, a contract asset is recognised for the earned consideration that is conditional. Trade Receivable represents the

g)	
A contract liability is recognised if a payment is received or a payment is due (whichever is earlier) from a customer before

2.16	
Earnings per share
	
Basic earnings per share is calculated by dividing the net profit or loss attributable to equity holders of the company by the 
weighted average number of equity shares outstanding during the year.
	
For the purpose of calculating diluted earnings per share, the net profit or loss for the year attributable to equity shareholders of 
the company and the weighted average number of shares outstanding during the year are adjusted for the effects of all dilutive 
potential equity shares.
2.17	
Taxation
	
Income tax expense represents the sum of the tax currently payable and deferred tax.
•	
Current tax
	
Current income tax assets and liabilities are measured at the amount expected to be recovered from or paid to the 
taxation authorities. The tax rates and tax laws used to compute the amount are those that are enacted or substantively 
enacted, at the reporting date. 
	
Current income tax relating to items recognised outside profit or loss is recognised outside profit or loss (either in other 
comprehensive income or in equity). Current tax items are recognised in correlation to the underlying transaction either in 
OCI or directly in equity. Management periodically evaluates positions taken in the tax returns with respect to situations 
in which applicable tax regulations are subject to interpretation and considers whether it is probable that a taxation 
authority will accept an uncertain tax treatment. The Group shall reflect the effect of uncertainty for each uncertain tax 
treatment by using either most likely method or expected value method, depending on which method predicts better 
resolution of the treatment.
•	
Deferred tax
	
Deferred tax is recognised using balance sheet approach on temporary differences between the carrying amounts of 
assets and liabilities in the financial statements and the corresponding tax bases used in the computation of taxable 
profit. Deferred tax liabilities are recognised for all taxable temporary differences. Deferred tax assets are recognised for 
all deductible temporary differences to the extent that it is probable that taxable profits will be available against which 
those deductible temporary differences can be utilized. Such deferred tax assets and liabilities are not recognised if the 
temporary difference arises from the initial recognition (other than in a business combination) of assets and liabilities in 
a transaction that affects neither the taxable profit nor the accounting profit and does not give rise to equal taxable and 
deductible temporary differences. 
	
Deferred tax assets are recognised for unused tax losses, unused tax credits and deductible temporary differences to 
the extent that it is probable that future taxable profits will be available against which they can be used. Future taxable 
profits are determined based on the reversal of relevant taxable temporary differences. If the amount of taxable temporary 
differences is insufficient to recognise a deferred tax asset in full, then future taxable profits, adjusted for reversals of 
existing temporary differences, are considered, based on the business plans for individual subsidiaries in the Group.
	
The carrying amount of deferred tax assets is reviewed at the end of each reporting period and reduced to the extent that 
it is no longer probable that sufficient taxable profits will be available to allow all or part of the asset to be recovered.
	
Unrecognised deferred tax assets are re-assessed at each reporting date and are recognised to the extent that it has 
become probable that future taxable profits will allow the deferred tax asset to be recovered.
	
Deferred tax liabilities and assets are measured at the tax rates that are expected to apply in the period in which the 
liability is settled or the asset is realized, based on tax rates (and tax laws) that have been enacted or substantively 
enacted by the end of the reporting period.
	
The Group offsets deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities if and only if it has a legally enforceable right to set off 
current tax assets and current tax liabilities and the deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities relate to income taxes 
levied by the same taxation authority on either the same taxable entity which intends either to settle current tax liabilities 
and assets on a net basis, or to realise the assets and settle the liabilities simultaneously, in each future period in which 
significant amounts of deferred tax liabilities or assets are expected to be settled or recovered.

•	
net interest expense or income; and

remeasurement

Remeasurement, comprising actuarial gains and losses, the effect of the changes to the asset ceiling (if applicable) and the

Short-term employee benefits including accumulated compensated absences as at the Balance Sheet date are recognised as

Liabilities recognised in respect of other long-term employee benefits are measured at the present value of the estimated future 
cash outflows expected to be made by the Group’s in respect of services provided by employees up to the reporting date.

Financial assets at amortised cost (debt instruments)
	
A ‘financial asset’ is measured at the amortised cost if both the following conditions are met:
•	
The asset is held within a business model whose objective is to hold assets for collecting contractual cash flows, and
•	
Contractual terms of the asset give rise on specified dates to cash flows that are solely payments of principal and interest 
(SPPI) on the principal amount outstanding.
	
This category is the most relevant to the Group. After initial measurement, such financial assets are subsequently measured 
at amortised cost using the effective interest rate (EIR) method and are subject to impairment as per the accounting policy 
applicable to ‘Impairment of financial assets. Amortised cost is calculated by taking into account any discount or premium on 
acquisition and fees or costs that are an integral part of the EIR. The EIR amortisation is included in other income in the profit or 
loss. The losses arising from impairment are recognised in the profit or loss. 
	
Financial assets at fair value through OCI (FVTOCI) (debt instruments)
	
A ‘financial asset’ is classified as at the FVTOCI if both of the following criteria are met:
•	
The objective of the business model is achieved both by collecting contractual cash flows and selling the financial assets, 
and
•	
The asset’s contractual cash flows represent SPPI.
	
Debt instruments included within the FVTOCI category are measured initially as well as at each reporting date at fair value. For 
debt instruments, at fair value through OCI, interest income, foreign exchange revaluation and impairment losses or reversals 
are recognised in the profit or loss and computed in the same manner as for financial assets measured at amortised cost. The 
remaining fair value changes are recognised in OCI. Upon derecognition, the cumulative fair value changes recognised in OCI is 
reclassified from the equity to profit or loss. 
	
Financial assets designated at fair value through OCI (equity instruments)
	
Upon initial recognition, the Group can elect to classify irrevocably its equity investments as equity instruments designated at 
fair value through OCI when they meet the definition of equity under Ind AS 32 Financial Instruments: Presentation and are 
not held for trading. The classification is determined on an instrument-by-instrument basis. Equity instruments which are held 
for trading and contingent consideration recognised by an acquirer in a business combination to which Ind AS103 applies are 
classified as at FVTPL.
	
Gains and losses on these financial assets are never recycled to profit or loss. However, on derecognition, the Company may 
transfer the cumulative gain or loss within equity.  Dividends are recognised as other income in the statement of profit and loss 
when the right of payment has been established, except when the Group benefits from such proceeds as a recovery of part of 
the cost of the financial asset, in which case, such gains are recorded in OCI. Equity instruments designated at fair value through 
OCI are not subject to impairment assessment.
	
Financial assets at fair value through profit or loss
	
Financial assets at fair value through profit or loss are carried in the balance sheet at fair value with net changes in fair value 
recognised under other income in the statement of profit and loss.

2.25.4	 Impairment of financial assets
	
The Group recognises an allowance for expected credit losses (ECLs) for all debt instruments not held at fair value through 
profit or loss. ECLs are based on the difference between the contractual cash flows due in accordance with the contract and 
all the cash flows that the Group expects to receive, discounted at an approximation of the original effective interest rate. The 
expected cash flows will include cash flows from the sale of collateral held or other credit enhancements that are integral to 
the contractual terms.
	
ECLs are recognised in two stages. For credit exposures, for which there has not been a significant increase in credit risk 
since initial recognition, ECLs are provided for credit losses that result from default events that are possible within the next 
12-months (a 12-month ECL). For those credit exposures for which there has been a significant increase in credit risk since 
initial recognition, a loss allowance is required for credit losses expected over the remaining life of the exposure, irrespective of 
the timing of the default (a lifetime ECL).
	
For trade receivables, the Group applies a simplified approach in calculating ECLs. Therefore, the Group does not track changes 
in credit risk, but instead recognises a loss allowance based on lifetime ECLs at each reporting date. The Group has established 
a provision matrix that is based on its historical credit loss experience, adjusted for forward-looking factors specific to the trade 
receivables and the economic environment.
	
For debt instruments at fair value through OCI, the Group applies the low credit risk simplification. At every reporting date, 
the Group evaluates whether the debt instrument is considered to have low credit risk using all reasonable and supportable 
information that is available without undue cost or effort. In making that evaluation, the Group reassesses the internal credit 
rating of the debt instrument.

Restoration, rehabilitation and 
environmental costs
Provision is made for costs associated with restoration and rehabilitation of mining sites 
as soon as the obligation to incur such costs arises. Such restoration and closure costs 
are typical of extractive industries, and they are normally incurred at the end of the life of 
the mine fields. The costs are estimated on the basis of mine closure plans with the help 
of third-party experts and the estimated discounted costs of dismantling and removing 
these facilities and the costs of restoration are capitalized when incurred reflecting the 
Group’s obligations at that time. 
Business combination
The Group determines whether an acquisition is business combination or an asset 
acquisition. As a part of the acquisition accounting, the Group measures all assets and 
liabilities as at the acquisition date at its fair values. The Group engaged an independent 
valuation specialist to assess fair values of tangible and intangible assets. The 
estimated useful life of tangible and intangible assets for such assets acquired as part 
of the business combination were considered based on economic life of those assets 
as estimated by the management basis a technical assessment. Goodwill as on the 
acquisition date is measured as the excess of the consideration transferred over the fair 
value of the net assets acquired.
The Group determines impairment for goodwill by assessing the recoverable amount of 
CGU to which such goodwill relates. When the recoverable amount of the CGU is less 
than its carrying amount, an impairment loss is recognised. The recoverable amount has 
been determined based on value in use. Value in use has been determined based on 
future cash flows, after considering current economic conditions and trends, estimated 
future operating results, growth rates and anticipated future.
The Group has a choice of performing optional concentration test for each acquisition 
after taking into consideration the nature of assets and activities acquired. In determining 
fair value of assets and liabilities acquired, the Group estimates future cash flows, 
growth rates, operating results etc.
2.31	
New and amended standards
	
The Group applied for the first-time certain standards and amendments, which are effective for annual periods beginning on or 
after 1 April 2025. The Group has not early adopted any standard, interpretation or amendment that has been issued but is not 
yet effective.
(i)	
Amendments to Ind AS 1 – Classification of Liabilities as Current or Non-current and Non-current Liabilities with 
Covenants
	
In August 2025, the MCA notified amendments to paragraphs 69 to 76 of Ind AS 1 to specify the requirements for 
classifying liabilities as current or non-current. The amendments are effective for annual reporting periods beginning 
on or after 1 April 2025 retrospectively in accordance with Ind AS 8.The amendments have not resulted in additional 
disclosures and have not had an impact on the classification of Group’s liabilities.
(ii)	
Amendments to Ind AS 7 and Ind AS 107 – Supplier Finance Arrangements
	
In August 2025, the MCA notified amendments to Ind AS 7 Statement of Cash Flows and Ind AS 107 Financial Instruments: 
Disclosures to clarify the characteristics of supplier finance arrangements and require additional disclosure of such 
arrangements. The disclosure requirements in the amendments are intended to assist users of financial statements in 
understanding the effects of supplier finance arrangements on an entity’s liabilities, cash flows and exposure to liquidity 
risk. 
	
As a result of implementing the amendments, the Group has provided additional disclosures about its supplier finance 
arrangements. Please refer note 2.26.3 and note 23A to the consolidated financial statements.
(iii)	
There are certain other amendments to Ind AS 12 Income Taxes and Ind AS 21 The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange 
Rates, which did not have any impact on the Company.

In accordance with Ind AS 109, the Group uses the expected credit loss (“ECL”) model for measurement and recognition of impairment loss 
on its trade receivables. For this purpose, the Group uses a provision matrix to compute the expected credit loss amount for trade receivables. 
The provision matrix takes into account external and internal credit risk factors and historical data of credit losses from various customers 
adjusted for forward looking estimates. Accordingly, the Group creates provision for past due receivables beyond 180 days ranging between 
25%-100% after reckoning the underlying collaterals. Besides, based on the expected credit loss model the Group also provides upto 0.5% 
for receivables less than 180 days.

Terms and conditions of supplier finance arrangement
The Group enters into deferred payment arrangements (acceptances) whereby overseas lenders such as banks and other financial institutions 
make payments to supplier’s banks for import of raw materials. The banks and financial institutions are subsequently repaid by the Group at a 
later date providing working capital benefits. These arrangements carry a weighted average interest rate of SOFR + spread p.a. as negotiated. 
These arrangements are a part of the facilities granted by finance providers which are secured by way of the Group’s current assets.

Considering the emerging practices on disclosures of trade credits and amendments to Ind AS 7/ Ind AS 107, the Group has reassessed its 
presentation of amount covered under supplier finance arrangement to provide more relevant information to the users of financial statements 
to assess impact of such arrangements on liabilities, cash flows and liquidity risks. Accordingly, interest bearing short-term acceptances in the 
nature of trade credits, which are within the normal working capital cycle of the Group, have been disclosed as a separate line under financial 
liabilities as Acceptances which was hitherto included in trade payables. The amount reflected as acceptances is Rs. 5,02,210 lakhs as at 
31 March 2026 (Rs. 3,06,182 lakhs and Rs. 2,99,792 lakhs as at 31 March 2025 and 1 April 2024 respectively). The reclassification does 
not have any material impact on information presented in the balance sheet at the beginning of the preceding period in so far it relates to 
Group’s liquidity, working capital and performance. The above changes do not impact recognition and measurement of items in the financial 
statements, and consequentially, there is no impact on total equity and/or profit/(loss) for the current or any of the earlier periods.These 
amounts are not due and undisputed as at the balance sheet date.

32.1 Capital management
The Group’s capital management objective is to maximise the total shareholder return by optimising cost of capital through flexible capital 
structure that supports growth. Further, the Group ensures optimal credit risk profile to maintain/enhance credit rating. 
The Group determines the amount of capital required on the basis of annual operating plan and long-term strategic plans. The funding 
requirements are met through internal accruals and long-term/short-term borrowings. The Group monitors the capital structure on the basis 
of Net debt to equity ratio and maturity profile of the overall debt portfolio of the Group. 
For the purpose of capital management, capital includes issued equity capital, securities premium and all other reserves. Net debt includes 
all long and short-term borrowings as reduced by cash and cash equivalents, Bank deposits and inter-corporate deposits with financial 
institutions.

b. 	
Commodity price risks	 	
	
	
	
	
The Group’s operating activities require the ongoing purchase of rock phosphates, phosphoric acid, sulphur and muriate of potash. All 
being international commodities are subject to price fluctuations on account of the change in the demand supply pattern and exchange 
rate fluctuations. The Company is generally not affected by the price volatility of the raw materials as government on a time to time basis, 
revises the subsidy rates payable to the fertilizer industry based on the market trend.The Group has considered uncertainties relating to the 
commodity prices in preparation of these financial statements.
32.5 Credit risk management	
Credit risk refers to the risk that a counterparty will default on its contractual obligations resulting in financial loss to the Group. The Group is 
exposed to credit risk from its operating activities (primarily trade receivables) and from its financing activities, including deposits with banks 
and financial institutions, foreign exchange transactions and other financial instruments.
Customer credit risk is managed by each business unit subject to the Group’s established policy, procedures and control relating to the 
customer credit risk management. The Group uses financial information and past experience to evaluate credit quality of majority of its 
customers and individual credit limits are defined in accordance with this assessment. Outstanding receivables and the credit worthiness of 
its counterparties are periodically monitored and taken up on case to case basis. The Group evaluates the concentration of risk with respect 
to trade receivables as low (except Government subsidies which is entirely receivable from Government of India), as its customers are located 
in several jurisdictions representing large number of low value eceivables operating in independent markets. 
The credit risk on cash and bank balances, derivative financial instruments is limited because the counterparties are banks with high credit 
ratings assigned by international credit rating agencies.
For details of financial guarantee, refer note 32.7.
32.6 Liquidity risk management
The Group manages liquidity risk by maintaining adequate reserves, banking facilities and reserve borrowing facilities, by continuously 
monitoring forecast and actual cash flows, and by matching the maturity profiles of financial assets and liabilities. Note 32.8 sets out details 
of additional undrawn facilities that the Company has at its disposal to reduce liquidity risk.

The four codes prescribe an inclusive definition of the term ‘wages’, which among other matters is relevant for determination of post-
employment benefits including gratuity to all employees. In accordance with the definition, certain specified items forming part of 
remuneration are not included in the wages and these excluded items cannot exceed 50% of total remuneration. If there is an excess, 
then it is presumed that excess amount also forms part of wages. The four codes also introduce changes related to leave entitlement 
and encashment for workers. Going forward, workers’ leave balance in excess of 30 days will be encashed at the end of each calendar 
year and workers will have a right to demand encashment for entire leave. 
	
The Group has assessed the impact of these changes on the basis of legal view obtained by the management and the best information 
available till authorisation of the financial statements for issue.  The Group has presented increase in obligation as an expense under the 
head “Employee Benefit Expense” in the consolidated statement of profit and loss for the year ended 31 March 2026. Considering that 
it is emerging topic and the finalisation of Central/ State Rules is still pending, the Group will continue monitoring changes and provide 
appropriate accounting effect as required based on future developments.

Reporting Landscape
How We Report and Create Value
1GRI 2-3
Coromandel International Limited (hereinafter referred 
to as “the Company”, “CIL”, or “Coromandel”) presents 
its Integrated Annual Report for FY 2025-26. The 
Report covers the Company’s financial, operational 
and environmental, social and governance (ESG) 
performance.
The objective of this Report is to provide a concise 
and integrated overview of Coromandel’s strategy, 
governance, performance and value creation process 
across financial and non financial capitals, enabling 
stakeholders to understand how the Company creates 
sustainable long term value.
Our Approach to Integrated Reporting
Coromandel International Limited (CIL) is one of India’s 
leading agri solutions providers, operating across the 
agricultural value chain with a focus on innovation, 
operational excellence and responsible practices.
This Integrated Report presents the Company’s 
financial and non financial performance for the year 
ended March 31, 2026, and ar

ticulates how Coromandel 
creates sustainable value for its stakeholders in 
alignment with its Vision, Mission and Values.
Coromandel’s integrated reporting approach brings 
together financial disclosures with environmental, 
social and governance (ESG) performance, enhancing 
transparency, 
comparability 
and 
decision 
useful 
insights for stakeholders, in line with leading global 
reporting practices.
Reporting Principles
This 
Integrated 
Report 
has 
been 
prepared 
in 
accordance with the principles of the International 
Integrated Reporting Council (IIRC). The disclosures are 
also aligned with the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) 
Standards and comply with the requirements of India’s 
Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting 
(BRSR) framework.
Through this approach, the Report supports alignment 
with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 
(UN SDGs) and reflects Coromandel’s commitment 
to transparent, relevant and globally comparable 
reporting.
Materiality
Coromandel identifies its material topics through a 
structured assessment process involving stakeholder 
engagement and internal evaluations. These topics are 
prioritised based on their relevance to the Company’s 
business strategy, long term value creation and 
stakeholder interests.
The identified material matters are evaluated with 
reference to globally recognised frameworks such as 
the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB), 
Dow Jones Sustainability Index (DJSI) and MSCI, 
ensuring comprehensive coverage of both financial and 
non financial impacts.
During 
FY 2025–26, 
Coromandel 
conducted 
a 
comprehensive materiality assessment exercise, the 
details and outcomes of which are presented in the 
section below.
Inclusivity
Coromandel emphasises accountability towards all 
stakeholders impacted directly or indirectly by its 
operations. Through structured stakeholder mapping, 
engagement and feedback mechanisms, the Company 
integrates stakeholder expectations

into its strategy, 
decision making and operations.
CIL continues to strengthen engagement across 
corporate, manufacturing, supply chain and marketing 
functions to foster collaboration and drive continuous 
improvement.
Scope and Reporting Boundary
This Integrated Report presents information for 
Coromandel International Limited on a standalone 
basis and covers all facilities operated by the Company 
across its businesses, including Fertilisers, Specialty 
Nutrients, Crop Protection, Retail and Specialty 
Chemicals.
Unless otherwise specified, the disclosures relate to 
Coromandel’s operations within India and encompass its 
economic, social and environmental performance. The 
reporting boundary extends to factors that materially 
influence the Company’s ability to create sustainable 
value over the short, medium and long term.
Reporting Period
This 
Integrated 
Report 
covers 
the 
period 
from 
April 1, 2025, to March 31, 2026. The Report is published 
on an annual basis.
Reliability of Data
Coromandel follows a robust verification framework 
to ensure the accuracy, completeness and reliability of 
information disclosed in this Report. The disclosures 
are supported by internal controls, periodic reviews and 
defined audit trails.
ESG data has been subjected to external assurance 
in accordance with the GRI Guidelines and ISAE 3000 
(revised), while BRSR Core disclosures have been 
assured in line with BRSR Assurance requirements and 
ISAE 3000 (revised), enhancing the credibility of the 
reported information.
Responsibility and Feedback Statement
The Report has been developed under the guidance and 
oversight of Coromandel’s Board of Directors in adherence 
to 
applicable 
regulatory 
frameworks. 
Stakeholder 
feedback is valued and welcomed to strengthen future 
disclosures.

Reflections from 
the Leadership
For more than six decades, Coromandel has been built 
on a simple conviction shared with the wider Murugappa 
Group: enduring growth comes from strong foundations, 
disciplined execution and the willingness to invest 
ahead of the curve. FY2025-26 reflected all three. In 
a year marked by external volatility, we continued to 
strengthen our core businesses, deliver on important 
strategic investments and build the capabilities required 
for the future. As several of these investments now move 
from execution to commissioning and operationalisation, 
our priorities are sharply defined: to translate them into 
value, stronger returns and sustainable cash flows, 
while continuing to scale the businesses that will shape

securing supply continuity and meeting a substantial share of the Kakinada plant’s acid requirements.
Creating India’s largest phosphatic fertiliser complex

serve markets across India efficiently, while producing high-quality, energy-efficient phosphatic fertilisers. The brownfield 
expansion is expected to be completed in FY27 and will support import substitution, particularly in the northern markets, 
thereby promoting balanced crop nutrition through NPK fertilisers.
Developing India’s first technical MAP water soluble fertiliser plant
Coromandel is advancing its innovation-led growth strategy through the development of India’s first technical MAP (Mono 
Ammonium Phosphate) water soluble fertiliser plant. This will strengthen the Company’s presence in the high-value specialty 
nutrients segment, catering to the growing demand for precision farming and fertigation solutions. With India currently 
dependent on imports for its entire MAP requirement, the project will enable import substitution, ensure reliable availability 
of high-quality MAP, and enhance self-reliance while supporting farmers with efficient, crop-specific nutrition.

Our Legacy and Evolution
Coromandel International Limited was incorporated in 1961 as Coromandel Fertilisers Limited, through a strategic 
collaboration between International Minerals and Chemical Corporation (USA), Chevron Chemical Company,

and EID Parry.

contributing meaningfully to India’s agricultural transformation during the Green Revolution.
Over the years, EID Parry progressively increased its shareholding, leading to Coromandel’s integration as a core company of 
the Murugappa Group, one of India’s most respected and diversified business conglomerates. This association strengthened 
Coromandel’s governance framework, long term vision, and its commitment to ethical and responsible business practices 
guided by the Group’s “Five Lights”.
From its origins as a fertiliser manufacturer, Coromandel has steadily evolved into an integrated agri solutions provider, 
expanding its capabilities across plant nutrients, crop protection, specialty and organic products, retail, and farm services. 
Today, its journey reflects a legacy of resilience and continuous transformation, focused on supporting Indian agriculture 
through innovation, scale, and sustainability.

Corporate Governance
The Company places Corporate Governance at the core of its operations, recognising it as fundamental to building stakeholder 
trust, ensuring long-term resilience, and enabling sustainable value creation. The Company’s governance framework is built 
on the principles of transparency, integrity, accountability, and ethical conduct, which guide decision-making and execution 
across all levels of the organisation.
The Company firmly beli

eves that strong governance is essential to delivering enduring value for a wide range of stakeholders, 
including shareholders, investors, employees, suppliers, regulators, farmers, and the communities it serves. Governance is 
embedded as a strategic enabler, ensuring that business decisions and actions are consistently aligned with applicable legal, 
regulatory, and ethical standards.
The Board of Directors provides strategic oversight and direction, while monitoring the effectiveness of management in driving 
performance with clarity, discipline, and accountability. Through this Integrated Annual Report, the Company presents a 
transparent and comprehensive view of its financial performance, governance practices, and sustainability initiatives, enabling 
stakeholders to clearly understand its long-term vision and value creation approach.
The following are the seven key corporate governance focus areas 
that the Company strongly emphasises:
Transparency & Ethical Disclosure
Company is committed to transparent, timely and accurate disclosures across financial and non financial 
matters. The Company upholds the highest standards of ethical reporting, ensuring stakeholders receive 
clear, credible and decision useful information in line with applicable laws and regulations.
Proactive Risk Management
The Company follows a structured and forward‑looking risk management framework to identify, assess 
and mitigate strategic, operational, financial and emerging risks. This proactive approach strengthens 
resilience and supports informed decision‑making in a dynamic business environment.
Robust Internal Controls
Company maintains a strong system of internal controls to safeguard assets, ensure the integrity of 
financial reporting and promote compliance. Regular reviews, audits and process enhancements reinforce 
accountability and operational discipline across the organisation.
Excellence in Product & Service Quality
Quality is embedded across Company’s value chain from

sourcing and manufacturing to service delivery. 
The Company continuously strengthens quality assurance systems to ensure consistent product 
performance, customer satisfaction and adherence to regulatory standards.
High Standards for Safety, Health & Environment (SHE)
Company places the highest priority on safety, employee well being and environmental stewardship. 
Stringent SHE practices, continuous monitoring and preventive initiatives are implemented to protect 
people, communities and natural resources.
Strategic Communication & Alignment
Effective communication and alignment across the Board, management and operational teams ensure 
clarity of purpose and consistency in execution. Coromandel promotes transparent engagement with 
stakeholders to align strategy, performance and long term objectives.
Financial Integrity & Accountability
The Company upholds strong financial discipline through prudent capital allocation, robust financial 
controls and responsible stewardship of resources. This ensures accountability, protects stakeholder 
interests and supports sustainable long term value creation.

Risk Management
Coromandel operates in a business environment shaped by agricultural cycles, commodity price movements, regulatory 
developments, climate variability, global supply chain dependencies and evolving expectations on environmental 
stewardship. As a diversified Agri-solutions company with businesses across fertilisers, crop protection, bioproducts, 
retail and farmer-facing services, the Company recognises that risk management is an important component to protecting 
operational continuity, financial performance, stakeholder confidence and long-term value creation.
The Company’s risk management approach is designed to support timely decision-making across strategic, operational, 
financial, regulatory, environmental and reputational matters. It enables the organisation to identify risks early, assess their 
likely impact, assign clear ownership and respond through defined mitigation plans. During the year, Coromandel continued 
to strengthen the linkage between Enterprise Risk Management, Business Continuity Management, emergency response 
and crisis preparedness, creating a more connected view of risk and resilience across corporate, divisional and plant levels.
The Company’s Enterprise Risk Management framework enables structured identification, assessment, prioritisation and 
mitigation of risks across corporate, divisional and plant levels. It also supports informed decision-making by linking key risks 
with strategy, operations, capital planning, compliance and business continuity. During the year, Coromandel continued to 
strengthen the connection between risk management, business resilience and crisis preparedness. This included a sharper 
focus on climate and nature-related risks, supply chain continuity, regulatory compli

ance, operational safety, cyber security, 
workforce availability and emerging market shifts.

Risks are identified through inputs from business plans, operational reviews,

Identified risks are categorised into priority levels based on their inherent risk

business continuity planning and corrective actions.

reviews are conducted at unit, divisional, functional and corporate levels to 
monitor key risks and emerging concerns.
The effectiveness of mitigation actions is reviewed by management and 
oversight committees. Material risks, residual exposures and unresolved actions 
are reported through defined governance channels for further direction.

Risk Governance
Coromandel’s risk governance structure is led by the Board of Directors, which provides oversight on key risks that may 
influence the Company’s strategy, operations, financial position, compliance obligations and stakeholder relationships. The 
Board is supported by its committees, including the Risk Manag

ement Committee, Audit Committee and Corporate Social 
Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, each of which reviews risk matters relevant to its mandate.
The Risk Management Committee plays a critical role in reviewing the Company’s enterprise risk profile, mitigation progress 
and emerging areas of concern. It also monitors the effectiveness of the risk management framework and guides the 
prioritisation of risks that require senior management attention. The Audit Committee complements this oversight through its 
review of internal controls, audit observations and control-related corrective actions.
At the management level, the Executive Management Team, comprising the Managing Director, Executive Directors and 
CXOs, is responsible for translating Board-level risk priorities into business action. Business Heads, Corporate Functions and 
the EHS leadership team are accountable for identifying, assessing and managing risks within their respective areas. Unit-
level Safety and Sustainability Committees further support implementation at operating sites, particularly for risks linked to 
safety, environment, climate resilience, compliance and business continuity.

Through FY 2025-26, Coromandel continued to strengthen 
the foundation of its manufacturing network, adding 
capacity in areas that consolidate competitive advantage 
and building capability in areas that accelerate future 
growth. Capital was deployed across four interlocking 
themes during the year, namely the strengthening of the 
crop protection franchise, the expansion of fertiliser capacity 
and raw material security, the deepening of the advanced 
and differentiated portfolio, and the long-term safeguarding 
of water resources.
Strengthening the crop protection
In a defining step for its crop protection business, 
Coromandel completed the acquisition of a 53.13% 
contro

lling stake in NACL Industries Limited for ₹820 
crore at ₹76.7 per share, following clearance from the 
Competition Commission of India in 2025. NACL brings to 
the portfolio an established branded formulation business 
in the domestic market, a technicals export base across key 
global markets and contract manufacturing relationships 
with leading global agrochemical companies, materially 
expanding Coromandel’s manufacturing footprint, product 
portfolio and operational scale in crop protection.
Manufacturing capability was further deepened for the 
manufacture of recently off patented fungicides, alongside 
a 9 KTPA technical plant at Dahej. Targeted capacity 
additions were also completed for key technical molecules 
at Ankleshwar and a herbicide block expansion at Sarigam.
Expanding fertiliser capacity and raw material 
security
At Kakinada, the Company advanced construction of a new 
NPK granulation train (Train H). On commissioning, Train 
H will add 7.5 lakh tonnes of annual capacity, taking the 
Kakinada site to 30 lakh tonnes per annum and positioning 
it among the largest phosphatic fertiliser complexes in 
India. The new train is being built using energy efficient, 
environmentally compliant technology and is designed to 
substitute DAP imports while improving balanced crop 
nutrition through complex NPKs.
Running in parallel, the previously announced backward 
integration investment of approximately ₹1,000 crore at 
Kakinada, comprising a 650 TPD phosphoric acid plant and 
a 2,000 TPD sulphuric acid plant, progressed as planned, 
this will bring all of Coromandel’s fertiliser manufacturing 
sites into a backward integrated configuration, reducing 
dependence on imports of intermediate raw materials.
Upstream raw material security was further reinforced 
through the commissioning of a fixed processing plant for 
Run of Mine (ROM) material at the Baobab Mining and 
Chemicals Corporation rock phosphate project in Senegal, 
in which Coromandel now holds a

53.8% stake. The 
fixed processing plant secures consistent rock phosphate 
feedstock for the Company’s phosphatic value chain and 
supports the upcoming phosphoric acid plant at Kakinada.
Deepening the advanced and differentiated 
portfolio
The advanced solutions portfolio was strengthened with 
a fully automated, energy efficient Nano Fertiliser Plant at 
Kakinada, featuring robotic bottling and an annual capacity 
of one crore bottles, with the platform designed to scale 
across multiple nano products. The differentiated portfolio 
was further extended through the commissioning of a 1.3 
lakh tonne Urea Single Super Phosphate facility at Nimrani 
in Madhya Pradesh, Udaipur, Rajasthan to manufacture 
Gromor Urea Super Phosphate (5:15:0:10), and the 
doubling of Bentonite Sulphur capacity at the Vizag unit to 
meet rising demand for secondary nutrients.
Securing water for the future
Reinforcing water security at one of its largest manufacturing 
hubs, Coromandel signed an agreement during the year 
with Veolia Water Technologies and Solutions (India) to 
expand seawater desalination capacity at Visakhapatnam 
from 6 MLD to 9 MLD, building on the 6 MLD plant 
commissioned in 2023. The expansion is being executed 
on a Build, Own, Operate model. On commissioning, the 
upgraded plant is expected to meet 60 to 70% of the site’s 
total water requirement, materially reducing dependence on 
freshwater sources and standing as a flagship achievement 
in operational sustainability and self-reliance.

During FY 2025-26, the CPC formulation R&D team developed recipes for 23 new combination products for domestic 
portfolio requirements and 21 novel combination products for export markets. In addition, products were developed for CDMO 
customers, with stability studies established to support their pro-gression toward commercialization. To further strengthen 
launch preparedness, the team advanced three combination formulations for launch readiness, including one fungicide and 
two insecticides.
Advancing Product Demonstration

and Commercialization  
As part of the product transition pathway from development to market deployment, formulations progressed to demonstration 
trials, of which four products were successfully commercialized during the year. These included CAVECO, INVICTO, DECIMATE 
& MALATHION 100 EC. In parallel, the packaging department completed container content compatibility studies for nine new 
combination products, supporting product stability and safe packaging validation. 
Reinforcing Quality and Compliance Capabilities  
During the year, the CPC R&D facility at Shamirpet underwent surveillance assessment by the NABL team covering 54 
products within scope, achieving 100% compliance with zero observations. This outcome reflects the robustness of laboratory 
systems supporting formulation development activities.

	» Enhanced regulatory and packaging readiness, lowering downstream execution bottlenecks.
	» Reinforced customer confidence through robust stability, compatibility, and quality systems. 
Value Created  
Through expanded formulation development, demonstration trials, commercialization progress and strengthened laboratory 
compliance performance, CPC R&D enhanced readiness across domestic and export product pipelines while supporting 
customer-specific requirements and packaging validation capabilities.

Enhancing Process Capability for Strategic Molecules
During FY 2025-26, Coromandel’s Crop Protection Chemicals (CPC) operations strengthened their manufacturing capability 
base through the development of scalable production processes for key technical molecules. Commercial scale processes 
were successfully established for multiple projects.

l, laboratory scale process development was completed for a set of advanced technicals and fluoro intermediates,

utilisation.
Scaling CDMO Engagements and Manufacturing Readiness 
The CPC team continued to build its position as a reliable manufacturing partner through Contract Development and 
Manufacturing Organisation (CDMO) engagements. Laboratory processes for CDMO projects were validated, and GLP

Coromandel’s capabilities in multi product manufacturing, flexible asset utilisation, and global supply integration.

applications, including two PCT applications. During the year, nine Indian patents were granted, reinforcing the organization’s

Value Created  
Through development of strategic technical molecules, advancement of CDMO collaborations, support for multi-geography 
registrations and expansion of the patent portfolio, CPC R&D strengthened its technical capability base and supported future

Role mapping and organization restructuring 
From a role-mapping perspective, Coromandel undertook a comprehensive organisational restructuring exercise during the 
last financial year in partnership with a global consulting agency with the aim of stre

ngthening its people processes, creating 
greater role clarity and building a scalable structure aligned with business growth. As part of this exercise, the Company’s 
earlier framework of 20 grades across 3 bands was revised to 19 grades across 6 bands.
Driven by senior leadership, the initiative was intended to make Coromandel a more agile organisation by redefining spans 
of control, roles and responsibilities and enabling faster career growth. Spanning several months, it involved extensive role 
mapping, outlier identification and benchmarking of the organisation structure against industry standards. Job evaluation was 
carried out using the Hays Methodology, a globally acclaimed and time-tested framework.
This restructuring has helped Coromandel establish a performance-driven culture, enable clearer career pathways, and create 
an organizational design that balances growth aspirations with operational efficiency.

At Coromandel, employee engagement and well-being are viewed as important enablers of operational performance, 
workforce stability and long-term growth. Given the Company’s presence across manufa

cturing units, field operations and

During the reporting year, the Company continued to enhance employee experience through engagement initiatives, accessible 
communication platforms and well-being programmes designed to address the evolving needs of its workforce. Coromandel’s 
approach centres on creating a workplace where employees are encouraged to share feedback, participate in organisational 
processes and contribute meaningfully to team and business outcomes.
Underpinning this approach is the recognition that employee well-being directly influences productivity, engagement and 
workplace morale. Initiatives therefore focus on physical health, mental resilience and social security, while also helping 
employees manage their work-life priorities more effectively.
Strengthening Employee Engagement 
Coromandel adopts a multi-layered approach to measuring 
employee engagement, ensuring that feedback is captured 
through both internal and external mechanisms. During 
FY 2025-26, the Company strengthened its engagement 
framework through internal perception surveys and 
external benchmarking assessments such as Great Place 
to Work and Mint Iconic Workplaces Survey, enabling real-
time feedback tracking as well as an independent view of 
workplace culture. 
This approach helped the Company understand employee 
sentiment across key aspects of workplace experience 
and identify areas where focused action is required. The 
insights gathered through these mechanisms support a 
more responsive engagement model, where employee 
feedback informs organisational priorities, location-level 
interventions and manager-led actions. 
Measuring Engagement: A Complimentary Approach
Employee engagement is assessed through internal and external complementary mechanisms:
	»
Great Place to Work (GPTW) Engagement Survey – conducted periodically to benchmark organisational culture aga

inst 
industry standards
	»
Mint Iconic Workplaces Survey – participated for the 1st time in past FY. The assessment facilitated by HT Media involved 
a multi-stage evaluation covering employee survey responses, AI-led interviews, and a review of people practices, followed 
by analysis by Deloitte and an independent jury evaluation.
	»
HR Internal Perception Survey (Quarterly) – conducted across locations to capture ongoing 
employee sentiment and track improvements at a granular level
The GPTW assessment focuses on the Trust Model consisting of 5 dimensions along which 
employee experiences at workplaces are assessed and forms the foundation of the Trust Index 
employee survey. The 5 dimensions are (i) Credibility, (ii) Respect, (iii) Fairness, (iv) Pride and (v) 
Camaraderie. The survey captures the responses covering aspects like job satisfaction, motivation, 
work life balance & stress management.
The Mint Iconic Workplaces survey measured 6 dimensions – Purposeful Work, Empowered 
Leadership, Thriving Environment, Collaborative Excellence, Inspiring Vision and Boundless Growth. 
The HR Internal Perception Survey measures 7 key dimensions consisting of HR Department 
Structure & Organisation, HR Planning & Organisational Development, Recruitment & Selection, 
Compensation & Performance Management, Employee Welfare & Benefits, Employee Relations & 
Communication, Training & Development.

Coromandel continues to place strong emphasis on employee well-being, recognising that a healthy, supported and engaged 
workforce is essential to sustained organisational performance. With a workforce of approximately ~6300 employees 
operating across manufacturing units, offices and field locations, the Company adopts a balanced approach that integrates 
policies, workplace flexibility and well-being initiatives to address diverse employee needs. 
The Company’s approach to well-being extends beyond traditional health measures to include physical, mental and social 
dimensions of employee welfare. During FY 2025-26, this commitment was reflected in over 100 well-being initiatives 
that reached employees across locations and functions. Participation across these programmes remained strong, with the 
Company’s flagship wellness platform, Bloom, recording around 75% participation and over 60% sustained engagement, 
indicating the growing adoption of healthier routines across the workforce.
The Company continues to focus on enabling policies that support employees through different life stages. Flexible working 
arrangements, childcare assistance post maternity leave and thoughtful leave policies have contributed to enhancing overall 
employee experience and accessibility to well-being resources.
Well-being in Action: Strengthening the ‘Bloom’ Platform 
As part of its continued focus on empl

oyee well-being, Coromandel has enhanced its flagship wellness platform, ‘Bloom’, 
which serves as a central pillar for driving employee participation, awareness and behavioural change across the organisation. 
Designed as an integrated well-being ecosystem, Bloom combines digital access with interventions to address multiple 
dimensions of employee health, including physical fitness, mental well-being and lifestyle management. The platform enables 
employees to engage with curated programmes, access expert-led sessions and adopt healthier routines in a structured and 
sustained manner. 
During FY 2025-26, the Company expanded the scope and reach of Bloom through targeted initiatives aimed at improving 
accessibility and driving deeper engagement across locations. Key initiatives under the Bloom programme included:
	»
Structured wellness sessions covering areas such as nutrition, physical fitness, stress management and mental 
well-being 
	»
Orientation and awareness sessions aimed at improving adoption and utilisation of the digital platform 
	»
Expert-led programmes encouraging employees to incorporate healthier routines into their daily lives 
	»
Health camps for employees ensuring continuous monitoring of health parameters. Unit level Medical Officers track 
employee health index periodically basis diagnostic testing and counsel employees on making lifestyle changes towards 
better health outcomes.
A recent addition to Bloom in line with women-centric initiatives was a Pregnancy Care program that women employees 
could sign up for, receiving dietary and fitness tips, easy access to specialists and groups where they could ask questions on 
their pregnancy journey and receive answers from medical experts. To further strengthen adoption, orientation and awareness 
sessions were conducted to familiarise employees with the platform and encourage regular participation. These efforts 
contributed to increased utilisation and visibility of the platform across the workfo

rce.
Building Connection Through Transparent and Inclusive 
Communication
Coromandel’s multi-tier Communication Framework ensures employees across locations and functions have consistent access 
to leadership, open dialogue and organisational direction. The framework operates across three integrated layers: leadership 
connect, content and digital reach, and structured listening.
Leadership Connect 
Chronicle, the Managing Director’s quarterly townhall, brings together employees across locations through 
business updates, MD Award recognitions and open Q&A sessions. CHORD complements this by enabling 
employees to connect directly with the Managing Director over a phone call each quarter to share ideas, 
feedback, process improvements and appreciation. Business and Departmental Townhalls, led by Business and 
Department Heads, translate organisational priorities into relevant local action, with Unit level communication 
meets further strengthening frontline leadership visibility. 
Content and Digital Reach 
VOICE Magazine, the Company’s award-winning internal publication, shares updates, achievements and 
employee stories from across business units. Coromandel maintains active engagement through LinkedIn, 
Instagram, YouTube and Facebook, while CASPER, its AI-powered HR chatbot, provides employees with policy 
guidance, ensuring accessibility and responsiveness across the workforce. 
Listening and Feedback 
Employee feedback is gathered through structured channels including the Great Place to Work survey, HR 
Internal Perception Survey, Engagement Champion conversations and HR Connects at locations/units. Insights 
are translated into action planning meetings with managers, monitored by the HR SPOCs at locations for 
accountability and timely action. A trained network of Engagement Champions facilitates ongoing team-level 
conversations across functions and locations. 
A key highlight of the year was the 22-day “BLOOMathon” step challenge, designed to promote physic

al activity 
and encourage sustained behavioural change. The initiative encouraged employees to achieve a daily target of 8,000 
steps and witnessed:
	»
Approximately 75% employee participation, reflecting strong engagement across functions and locations. 
	»
Over 60% sustained participation, indicating consistent involvement and the adoption of healthier habits.
Employee Benefits and Social Security 
Coromandel continues to provide a comprehensive benefits framework aimed at ensuring financial security, risk protection 
and long-term well-being for its employees. The Company’s approach is designed to go beyond statutory requirements, 
offering a balanced mix of protection-oriented and long-term financial benefits that support employees across different 
stages of their careers. 
All permanent employees are covered under a range of benefit programmes that contribute to their financial stability and 
overall well-being. These include accident insurance coverage, retirement provisions and schemes aligned with gratuity and 
superannuation benefits, providing support both during active employment and over the long term. This framework is further 
reinforced by statutory schemes such as the Employee Deposit Linked Insurance (EDLI), along with other group insurance 
programmes. Coverage is extended in line with defined eligibility criteria and employee grades, so that benefits remain 
equitable and relevant across the organisation.
Leave, Flexibility and Life-Stage Support
Coromandel continues to strengthen its human capital practices by embedding flexibility, inclusivity and life-stage support 
into its workplace framework. The Company recognises that employees operate within diverse personal and professional 
contexts and therefore require a work environment that is both structured and adaptable to evolving needs. Reflecting this, 
its leave and flexibility framework is designed not merely as a compliance requirement but as a strategic enabler of sustained 
employee eng

agement, career continuity and workforce resilience. By integrating statutory provisions with progressive policies 
and practical support mechanisms, the Company helps employees navigate critical life events while remaining meaningfully 
connected to the organisation.
A key component of the Company’s framework is Group Personal Accident Insurance, which provides compensation 
for total permanent disablement equivalent to 50 times the monthly gross salary for eligible employees. In addition, 
support is extended in cases of temporary disablement, including weekly compensation of ₹15,000 for a period of up 
to 104 weeks, ensuring income continuity during periods of absence.
In parallel, the Company offers retirement and long-term savings benefits, with Provident Fund coverage extended 
to all permanent employees. Superannuation Fund (SAF) benefits are available to eligible employees based on 
individual participation, supporting long-term financial planning and retirement preparedness. Employees are also 
covered under gratuity-linked benefits, where entitlements are linked to the completed service period. In certain 
cases, additional provisions extend benefits to cover the remaining service period up to the age of 58 years for eligible 
employees who have opted for SAF, providing enhanced financial security to employees and their families. The Group 
Term life Insurance policy offers income protection for family and covers all employee categories including contract 
labour, while the Benevolent Fund scheme offers immediate assistance in case of an employee’s death while in service.

While return to work rates for both genders continues to remain consistently high, the Company is progressively strengthening

To enable a smoother and more structured transition post Maternity Leave, Coromandel has implemented targeted support

ing on personal priorities.

maintaining continuity in roles and responsibilities.

towards family support  
Coromandel actively monitors parental leave utilisation and post-leave outcomes to assess the effectiveness of its policies

Process Safety Management and Responsible Operations
For Coromandel, process safety is central to responsible manufacturing. The Company’s operations involve chemicals and 
critical utilities such as ammonia, sulphuric acid, phosphoric acid, high-pressure steam, instrument air and vacuum systems, 
making disciplined risk management essential for protecting people, communities, assets and the environment.

involved in process operations and high-risk work are trained to understand process hazards, follow defined

Notice and Consultation on Operational Changes
When significant operational changes arise, the Company follows a systematic approach to communication and compliance. A 
minimum notice period is provided to employees in line with applicable statutory requirements, typically ranging between 21 
to 42 days depending on the nature of the change, employee category and regulatory provisions, ensuring that employees are 
adequately informed and supported during any transition. Where applicable, these provisions are aligned with agreements 
established with trade unions and employee representatives, so that workforce-related decisions are undertaken in 
consultation and in accordance with mutually agreed terms. During FY 2025-26, no significant operational changes requiring 
advance workforce notice arose.

Coromandel’s approach to community development is rooted in the belief that meaningful growth must also strengthen 
the communities around its operations. The Company’s CSR programmes are designed to respond to real needs on the 
ground, especially in the regions surrounding its plants, markets and retail networks. These initiatives are shaped through 
regular engagement with community members, village opinion leaders, local stakeholders and field teams, ensuring that 
interventions remain relevant, practical and responsive. Before commencing projects, the Company engages with community 
members and PRI representatives, seeking request or consent letters wherever applicable to ensure local alignment and 
ownership. Concerns raised by communities during regular interactions are recorded and addressed by the CSR team, with 
responsibility for community relations assigned to relevant executives as part of their project-level KRAs.
The Company follows a structured process to identify and prioritise CSR projects. Need assessment studies at plant locations, 
stakeholder meetings and continuous community interactions help capture local priorities. Based on these inputs, CSR 
programmes are planned and placed before the CSR Committee for review. Priority is given to projects that address urgent 
community needs and create wider public benefit. 
Coromandel’s CSR governance is guided by strong oversight from the CSR Committee and the Board of Directors. The Board 
approves the CSR Policy and provides strategic direction for key initiatives, while the CSR Committee oversees the formulation, 
review, approval and implementation of CSR programmes and the annual action plan. The

Committee also guides the CSR 
team wherever required, ensuring that all programmes remain aligned with the approved framework, statutory requirements 
and the Company’s broader responsibility agenda.
Implementation is supported by a continuous monitoring mechanism. At the field level, project execution is regularly reviewed 
by the CSR team through formal and informal interactions with community members. Monthly reports and plans are shared 
with the CSR Head and senior executives at plant locations, and progress is also presented to senior leadership at the 
Company level. Feedback received through these reviews is used to make required changes in ongoing CSR programmes, 
enabling the Company to improve outcomes and respond to evolving community needs. 
Coromandel  also undertakes third-party impact assessments to evaluate the effectiveness of its CSR initiatives. These 
assessments help record community feedback, understand the impact created through various projects and capture any 
grievances related to programme implementation. This strengthens transparency, accountability and learning across the CSR 
portfolio.

initiatives across locations. These honours reflect the Company’s continued contribution to rural development, health,

Coromandel Hospital, Kakinada: Healthcare as a Right, 
not a Privilege
At Coromandel, our sense of responsibility has always reached beyond the fields we serve and the nutrients we provide, into 
the wellbeing of the communities that sustain our business. We believe that access to high-quality, ethical healthcare is a 
fundamental right—one that should never depend on where a person lives or what they can afford. Coromandel Hospital in 
Kakinada is the most enduring expression of that conviction.
The institution began modestly in 2015 as a small medical centre in a rented building, with a few rooms, basic facilities and 
a compact team of committed healthcare professionals. What it lacked in scale, it met with dedication and a clear purpose: to 
place dependable medical care within reach of the underserved.
Over the past decade, that beginning has grown into a premier 60-bed, multi-specialty institution. The hospital was upgraded 
to a multi-specialty facility in 2021, and the inauguration of its integrated facility in 2026 marked a further step in deepening 
the care available locally. Today, Coromandel Hospital has served more than 3.44 lakh patients across the Kakinada, Dr. B.R. 
Ambedkar Konaseema and East Godavari districts, with over 600 individuals placing their trust in the institution each day—
from new mothers and elderly patients in chronic care to families navigating critical moments of their lives.
A central commitment has been to ensure that advanced medical infrastructure is available close to home, sparing families 
long and exhausting journeys to metro

politan centres. The hospital introduced the region’s first helium-free MRI—not as a 
showpiece, but in the belief that early, precise diagnosis saves lives and that a farming family in Konaseema deserves the 
same standard of imaging as anyone in a major city. This is supported by three fully equipped modular operation theatres, 
an eight-bed Medical Intensive Care Unit (MICU), a dedicated Surgical Intensive Care Unit (SICU) and a specialised Neonatal 
Intensive Care Unit (NICU).
The people of the region are the hospital’s true builders. Their trust, and their choice to rely on our doctors, nurses and staff 
in moments that matter most, remain its most valuable asset. To every family within its 100-kilometre service radius, the 
hospital extends a simple, lasting promise: to be present, to treat with uncompromising compassion, and never to place profit 
above wellbeing.
Looking ahead, Coromandel will continue to invest in modern technology, specialised medical talent and patient-centred 
services, so that no one in the region is ever forced to choose between their health and their savings. Sustained by care,

UDAN Masti Ki Pathshala: Giving Wings to Childhood in Migrant Communities
In the industrial corridors of Ankleshwar GIDC, where migrant families from Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Gujarat 
power factories and construction sites, education had quietly slipped to the margins of childhood. The seed for UDAN was 
sown during a Women’s Day celebration at Coromandel’s Ankleshwar Plant, when Maladevi, a widowed migrant worker, 
asked a deceptively simple question: could something be done to help educate their children? A community visit revealed that 
her concern was far from isolated. More than 150 children in the settlement were either out of school, irregular in attendance, 
or at risk of dropping out, hemmed in by language barriers, financial constraints and the absence of a nearby government 
primary school.

programme established Learning Centres within the migrant settlements themselves, replacing rote pedagogy with activity 
based, joyful learning focused on foundational literacy, numeracy and school readiness. What began with three centres 
grew organically to six on the strength of community demand alone. Over the year, 489 children were enrolled, more than 
350 attended regularly, and 30 children, many for the first time in their lives, transitioned into mainstream schools through

rather than passive recipients, and barriers that conventional programmes often overlook, such as language exclusion, migrant 
identity, low parental literacy and fragile home learning environments, are addressed directly. For Coromandel, the initiative 
illustrates how CSR can move beyond infrastructure or service delivery to respond to deeply embedded social inequities 
through empathy led design, gradually disrupting an intergenerational pattern of educational exclusion. In neighbourhoods 
where schooling once felt distant, it now exists within reach, and a widow’s question is being answered not through charity, 
but through opportunity.

ers between volunteers and classrooms, the programme positioned employees not as substitute teachers
